source_refs.note: 1.1.5 Argand Diagram with Figure (i), Modulus of Complex Number with Figure (ii), Example 3 (book p. 4-5, stops before EXERCISE 1.1); PDF 9-10.

blocks.text: Every complex number is represented by one and only one point of the coordinate plane, and every point of the plane represents one and only one complex number. The components of the complex number are the coordinates of the point representing it. In this representation the \(x\)-axis is called the real axis and the \(y\)-axis is called the imaginary axis. The coordinate plane itself is called the complex plane or \(z\)-plane. The figure representing one or more complex numbers on the complex plane is called an Argand diagram. The Argand diagram is a way of representing one or more complex numbers on the complex plane. Points on the \(x\)-axis represent real numbers, whereas points on the \(y\)-axis represent imaginary numbers.

blocks.alt: Argand diagram: x-axis is the real axis, y-axis the imaginary axis, both marked from -4 to 4. Points A(3, 2), B(-2, 2), C(-3, -2) and D(2, -2) are plotted, one in each quadrant.
blocks.caption: Figure (i): the complex numbers 3 + 2i, -2 + 2i, -3 - 2i and 2 - 2i as points A, B, C, D (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.text: In an Argand diagram the complex number \(x + iy\) is uniquely represented by the ordered pair \((x, y)\). In Figure (i), the complex numbers \(3 + 2i\), \(-2 + 2i\), \(-3 - 2i\) and \(2 - 2i\), which correspond to the ordered pairs \((3, 2)\), \((-2, 2)\), \((-3, -2)\) and \((2, -2)\), are represented geometrically by the points \(A\), \(B\), \(C\) and \(D\) respectively.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
How to plot \(x + iy\): start at the origin \(O\), move \(x\) units along the real axis (right if positive, left if negative), then \(y\) units parallel to the imaginary axis (up if positive, down if negative).
For \(-3 - 2i\): 3 units left, 2 units down: point \(C\).
A number and its conjugate are mirror images in the real axis: \(3 + 2i\) at \((3, 2)\) and \(3 - 2i\) at \((3, -2)\).

The real number \(\sqrt{x^2 + y^2}\) is called the modulus of the complex number \(x + iy\) and it is denoted by \(|x + iy|\). In Figure (ii), \(|\overline{OA}|\) represents the modulus of \(x + iy\). In other words, the modulus of a complex number is the distance from the origin to the point representing the number.

blocks.text_alt: the modulus of x plus i y equals the square root of x squared plus y squared

blocks.alt: Point A(x, y) in the complex plane joined to the origin O. AM is perpendicular to the x-axis, OM = x, MA = y, and OA, labelled square root of x squared plus y squared, is the modulus.
blocks.caption: Figure (ii): |OA| = square root of (x squared + y squared) is the modulus of x + iy (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why this formula? In Figure (ii), triangle \(OMA\) has a right angle at \(M\), with \(OM = x\) and \(MA = y\). By Pythagoras' theorem:
\[OA^2 = x^2 + y^2\]
\[OA = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}\]
Illustration (ours): \(|3 + 4i| = \sqrt{9 + 16} = \sqrt{25} = 5\), and \(|3 - 4i| = 5\) too.
The modulus is a real number and is never negative. It is 0 only for \(z = 0\).

blocks.caption: Moduli of the points of Figure (i) (our worked table)

blocks.title: Example 3
steps:
Given: \(z = \frac{(1+2i)^2}{2-i}\).
To find: \(|\overline{z}|\).
Method: first simplify \(z\) to the form \(x + iy\) (divide using the conjugate), then write \(\overline{z}\), and finally use the modulus formula \(|x + iy| = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}\).

Step 1: expand the square in the numerator
\[(1+2i)^2 = 1 + 4i + 4i^2\]
\[= 1 + 4i - 4\]
\[= -3 + 4i\]
Why: \((a+b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2\), and \((2i)^2 = 4i^2 = -4\).

Step 2: multiply top and bottom by the conjugate \(2 + i\)
\[z = \dfrac{-3 + 4i}{2 - i} \times \dfrac{2 + i}{2 + i}\]
Why: this makes the denominator real; multiplying by \(\frac{2+i}{2+i} = 1\) does not change the value.

Step 3: the numerator
\[(-3 + 4i)(2 + i)\]
\[= -6 - 3i + 8i + 4i^2\]
\[= -6 + 5i - 4\]
\[= -10 + 5i\]
Why: each term times each term, then \(4i^2 = -4\).

Step 5: find \(z\)
\[z = \dfrac{-10 + 5i}{5}\]
\[\Rightarrow z = -2 + i\]
Why: both parts are divided by 5.

Step 6: take the conjugate
The book prints: \(\overline{z} = \overline{-2-i} = -2+i\)
Working it out from \(z = -2 + i\):
\[\overline{z} = \overline{-2+i}\]
\[\overline{z} = -2 - i\]
Why: the conjugate keeps the real part \(-2\) and changes only the sign of the imaginary part, so \(+i\) becomes \(-i\).

Step 7: the modulus
\[|\overline{z}| = |-2 - i|\]
\[= \sqrt{(-2)^2 + (-1)^2}\]
\[= \sqrt{4 + 1}\]
\[|\overline{z}| = \sqrt{5}\]
Why: in \(|x + iy| = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}\) put \(x = -2\), \(y = -1\); squaring removes the minus signs.

Check:
\[(-2 + i)(2 - i) = -4 + 2i + 2i - i^2\]
\[= -4 + 1 + 4i\]
\[= -3 + 4i\]
This is \((1+2i)^2\), so \(z = -2 + i\) is right. Also \(|z| = \sqrt{4 + 1} = \sqrt{5}\): a number and its conjugate always have the same modulus.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book prints \(\overline{z} = \overline{-2-i} = -2+i\). Since \(z = -2 + i\), the correct line is \(\overline{z} = \overline{-2+i} = -2 - i\). The book's next line uses \(|-2 - i|\), so the final answer \(|\overline{z}| = \sqrt{5}\) is correct.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. Each complex number \(x + iy\) is exactly one point \((x, y)\) of the plane, and each point is exactly one complex number.
2. \(x\)-axis = real axis, \(y\)-axis = imaginary axis; the plane is the complex plane (\(z\)-plane).
3. \(|x + iy| = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}\) = distance of the point from the origin.
4. \(|\overline{z}| = |z|\).

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.text:
Putting \(i\) inside the formula: \(|3 + 4i| \ne \sqrt{9 + (4i)^2}\). Use \(y = 4\), not \(4i\).
Ignoring signs when squaring: \(|3 - 4i| = \sqrt{3^2 + (-4)^2} = \sqrt{9 + 16}\), not \(\sqrt{9 - 16}\).
Plotting \(x + iy\) at \((y, x)\): the real part always goes on the horizontal axis.
Taking the conjugate of the wrong number: in Example 3 the book writes the bar over \(-2-i\) instead of over \(z=-2+i\). Write \(z\) first, then change only the sign of its imaginary part.
